title: The baptism rite
hook: water, oil, a white garment, a lit candle, and a name

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new word: rite, worship done with the body as well as said. Your line was bodies remember. Which of your own small patterns did you do slowly, on purpose? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-three.

Five things on a small table near the font. A pitcher of water. A little vessel of oil. A folded white cloth. A tall candle, already burning. And a card with a name written on it. A family stands close, holding a baby who has no idea what's about to happen. Or it's a grown woman in a white robe, standing at the edge of a pool, shaking a little. In the Catholic and Orthodox rites, and in some others, all five things show up. In other churches it's water and a name, and nothing more. Either way, it's the rite that starts a Christian life. Today's word: the baptism rite.
screen: `A BABY, OR A GROWN WOMAN AT A POOL.`

segments.voice: Back in year one, this path looked at when churches baptize, infants or believers, and why. Today is about what the rite does with its hands. First, the water, at the center of every version described here. Paul says the person going under is joining Jesus in his death and coming up with him: "buried with him by baptism into death," so that "we also should walk in newness of life." Down, and up. Some churches plunge the whole body. Some pour. Some sprinkle. The picture underneath is the same. Second, the name. Often a minister asks the parents, or the person, what name they give, and says it aloud over the water. Isaiah has God say to Israel, "I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." A name spoken in front of everyone, tied to a promise. Third, the white garment. Paul writes, "as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ." Put on, like clothes. So in some churches the newly baptized are dressed in white, or a white cloth is laid on the baby. The clothes say what the water did. Fourth, the candle. Often it's lit from a larger candle that stands for the risen Christ, and handed to the family. Jesus told his followers, "Ye are the light of the world." And Paul writes, "ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord." So the rite ends with a flame in a parent's hand, and a job: keep it going. Water, a name, a garment, a light. A whole sermon, preached without a word of sermon, with things you can touch.

Here's the practice: light a candle, for your baptism if you were baptized, or for your birth if you weren't. If there's no candle nearby, a lamp works, or just a hand held open. Settle, and breathe. Look at the flame. Say your own name, quietly, the way someone said it over you once. Then think about who was there at the start: the people who held you, who named you, who hoped things for you before you could hope anything. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, just hold them in mind while the light burns. The bell holds the time.
The baptism rite. Water, a name, a white garment, a candle: the things a church uses to mark the start of a Christian life.

Your line: clothed in light. Today, when you get dressed, or put on a coat, let that be a small reminder of the white garment, and of whoever first called you by your name. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Christians baptize with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; Catholic, Orthodox and some other churches add anointing with oil, a white garment and a lit candle, while other churches keep the rite to water and words.

what it means: a rite in four signs: water for dying and rising, a name, a white garment, a lit candle.
what a scholar hears: Paul's "put on Christ" uses a clothing verb, so the white garment acts out his sentence; the robe says what the water did.

notes: Editor: the minister's question is now paraphrased without quotation marks, since it is not a public-domain wording.

Rite details: the Catholic Rite of Baptism includes anointing with chrism, a white garment and a candle lit from the Paschal candle; the Orthodox rite includes anointing, a white garment and candles. Stated as 'in the Catholic and Orthodox rites, and in some others'; confirm, and confirm the Orthodox details.
'What name do you give?' is paraphrased from the Catholic rite's opening question to parents ('What name do you give your child?'); presented as 'often' asked. Confirm.
Water is described as 'at the center of every version described here'; some groups (e.g., Quakers, Salvation Army) do not practice water baptism, which this day does not address.
Year one (day 152) covered infant vs believer baptism; today avoids repeating that angle.
Original: ἐνεδύσασθε is the verb form in Galatians 3:27; confirm spelling, accent and pronunciation.
